summary: The note is a wiki-style article on asphyxia, a condition of deficient oxygen supply caused by abnormal breathing that leads to generalized hypoxia, coma or death. It lists many causes, including airway obstruction, oxygen-poor environments, carbon monoxide and chemical exposure, drowning, and hanging. It then describes smothering, compressive asphyxia (including crowd crush disasters), perinatal asphyxia in newborns, competing definitions of mechanical asphyxia, and first aid steps for choking.
one_line: Overview of asphyxia, its causes, types including smothering and compressive and perinatal asphyxia, and first aid.
key_facts: Asphyxia or asphyxiation is a condition of deficient supply of oxygen to the body which arises from abnormal breathing.
Asphyxia causes generalized hypoxia, which affects all the tissues and organs, some more rapidly than others.
Asphyxia can cause coma or death.
In 2015, about 9.8 million cases of unintentional suffocation occurred which resulted in 35,600 deaths.
The word asphyxia is from Ancient Greek α- "without" and σφύξις sphyxis, "squeeze" (throb of heart).
Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity than oxygen to the hemoglobin in the blood's red blood corpuscles, bonding with it tenaciously, and, in the process, displacing oxygen.
Smothering is a mechanical obstruction of the flow of air from the environment into the mouth and/or nostrils, for instance by covering the mouth and nose with a hand, pillow, or a plastic bag.
The term "burking" comes from the method William Burke and William Hare used to kill their victims during the West Port murders.
Compressive asphyxia (also called chest compression) is mechanically limiting expansion of the lungs by compressing the torso, preventing breathing.
In the Hillsborough disaster in 1989, 97 Liverpool fans were crushed to death in an overcrowded terrace, 95 of the 97 from compressive asphyxia.
The Ibrox disaster in 1971 killed 66 Rangers fans, and the Luzhniki disaster in 1982 killed 66 FC Spartak Moscow fans.
Perinatal asphyxia is the medical condition resulting from deprivation of oxygen (hypoxia) to a newborn infant long enough to cause apparent harm.
Research by Ola Didrik Saugstad and others led to new international guidelines on newborn resuscitation in 2010, recommending the use of normal air instead of 100% oxygen.

In 2010, Sauvageau and Boghossian proposed that mechanical asphyxia be defined as caused by "restriction of respiratory movements, either by the position of the body or by external chest compression".
For first aid for mechanical asphyxia, the note advises standing behind the affected person, wrapping your arms around them, and pushing inwards and upwards under the ribs with a sudden movement.
